title: Different answers in the classical world
summary: The easiest mistake in comparing Rome, Han, India and Maya is to ask immediately which was stronger. Their geography, transport, populations and historical conditions differed. They were not competing in a shared race toward the modern state.

blocks.text: The easiest mistake in comparing Rome, Han, India and Maya is to ask immediately which was stronger. Their geography, transport, populations and historical conditions differed. They were not competing in a shared race toward the modern state.

More useful questions concern how large societies persisted. How did political institutions coordinate localities, knowledge survive, resources move and groups remain connected? Shared questions enable comparison without requiring identical institutional answers.

blocks.caption: Roman Empire · Context illustration; historical interpretation is in the text.

blocks.text: Time must also be specified. A broad window for examining classical civilizations does not imply synchronized development. Comparing one empire at its height with another society in crisis can manufacture a hierarchy that the comparison already assumed.

The classical world left several mature combinations. Cities and empires, bureaucracy and texts, multiple centers and local politics could perform different functions. The Atlas should make these differences understandable rather than compress them into a ranking.
